Buttock lines locate points to the right or left of the fuselage centerline. Wing stations are measurements along the span of the wing, with wing station zero the centerline of the fuselage.

ch05/jep-fig5-30.cap: Figure 5-30. A 45 degree angle is formed by a right triangle having two sides of equal length.

ch05/jep-fig5-31.cap: Figure 5-31. The steps for drawing a cube are simple when broken down into a step-by-step process.

ch05/jep-fig5-32.cap: Figure 5-32. A cylinder, cone, and sphere all take a three-dimensional look when shading is applied correctly.

ch05/jep-fig5-33.cap: Figure 5-33. By drawing arcs A,-A, and B,-B, and connecting their intersections, the center of line A-B is located.

ch05/jep-fig5-34.cap: Figure 5-34. To find the center of a circle, draw two chord lines, and their corresponding perpendicular bisectors.

ch05/jep-fig5-35.cap: Figure 5-35. Drawing a line through a point that is perpendicular to a baseline requires you to draw 2 sets of arcs.

ch05/jep-fig5-36.cap: Figure 5-36. Dividing a line into an equal number of parts requires a line of even length that is drawn diagonally from the original line.

ch05/jep-fig5-37.cap: Figure 5-37. To draw line A-D, draw arcs 1 and 2, then arc 1a-b and 2a-b. The line drawn from the intersection of arcs 3 and 4 to point A is the bisecting line.

ch05/jep-fig5-39.cap: Figure 5-39. To begin, locate the column on the left side of the chart representing a 28 volt system (item 1). Move down in this column until you find the horizontal line representing a wire length of 25 feet (item 2). Follow this line to the right until it intersects the diagonal line for 125 amps (item 3). Because the wire is in a bundle and carries a continuous current, you must be at or above curve 1 on the chart (item 4). Follow along the diagonal line representing 125 amps until it intersects curve 1 (item 5). From this point, drop down vertically to the bottom of the chart. The line falls between wire sizes 1 and 1/0 (item 6). Whenever the chart indicates a wire size between two sizes, you must select the larger wire. In this case, a 1/0, or single aught wire is required.

ch05/jep-fig5-40.cap: Figure 5-40. To calculate the brake mean effective pressure, BMEP, begin by locating 1,500 brake-horsepower on the top of the chart. From this value, drop down vertically until youreach the line representing 2,000 cubic inches of displacement. From this intersection, extend a line horizontally to the right until you intercept the line representing 2,400 rpm. Now, drop down vertically to read the brake mean effective pressure on the bottom line of the chart. The brake mean effective pressure is approximately 248.

ch05/jep-fig5-41.cap: Figure 5-41. To determine fuel consumption for an engine operating at 2,400 rpm, you must first determine the specific fuel consumption. To do this, locate 2,400 rpm on the bottom of the chart and follow the line up until it intersects the propeller load specific fuel consumption curve. From this intersection, extend a line to the right side of the chart and read a specific fuel consumption of .47 LB/ BHP/HR. Now, go back to the bottom of the chart and locate 2,400 rpm again. From this point move up to the propeller load horsepower curve. From this intersection, extend a line to the left side of the chart and read the brake horsepower of 127 hp. To determine the fuel burn, multiply the specific fuel consumption by the brake horsepower. The engine burns 59.69 pounds per hour (.47 x 127 = 59.69).

ch05/jep-fig5-42.cap: Figure 5-42. To determine the percent of sea level horsepower developed at an altitude of 7,000 feet, begin by finding the point on the horizontal axis that represents the desired altitude. From this point, move upward until you intersect the horsepower curve. Then move horizontally left to the chart's vertical axis and read the percent of sea level horsepower available.

ch06/jep-fig6-1.cap: Figure 6-1. Once the reference datum is set, all measurements to the right are positive, while all measurements to the left are negative.

ch06/jep-fig6-2.cap: Figure 6-2. The small child on the large arm balances the large child on the short arm.

ch06/jep-fig6-3.cap: Figure 6-3. A lever problem is simplified if you draw a picture of the problem and construct a chart. Notice that weight A is used as a datum.

ch06/jep-fig6-4.cap: Figure 6-4. Weight A has an arm of negative eight feet, and a corresponding moment of negative 200 pound-feet. The arm of weight B is a positive four feet, and has a moment of 200 pound-feet. The sum of the moments is zero and, therefore, the board balances.

ch06/jep-fig6-5.cap: Figure 6-5. The moment of A is +150 pound-feet, whereas, the moment of weight B is +900 pound-feet. This equates to a total moment of +1,050 pound-feet. When this is divided by the total weight, the balance point is found to be 14 feet to the right of the datum. This is the same location found in the previous example, eight feet to the right of weight A.

ch06/jep-fig6-7.cap: Figure 6-7. The sum of the moments left of the fulcrum is —1,800 pound-inches, and the moment right of the fulcrum is +1,800 pound-inches, therefore, the board balances.

ch06/jep-fig6-8.cap: Figure 6-8. An aircraft's Type Certificate Data Sheets contain information necessary to perform a weight and balance.

ch06/jep-fig6-9.cap: Figure 6-9. The platform scales used to weigh small aircraft are specially built with low beams to allow them to fit under low-wing aircraft.

ch06/jep-fig6-10.cap: Figure 6-10. The leveling means for an aircraft are specified in its Type Certificate Data Sheets.

ch06/jep-fig6-11.cap: Figure 6-11. A typical weighing form is useful to systematically record all weighing information.

ch06/jep-fig6-12.cap: Figure 6-12. The formulas for locating the centerline of an aircraft are based on the type of wheel configuration the aircraft has.

ch06/jep-fig6-13.cap: Figure 6-13. Itis often easier to compute weight and balance information when a picture is drawn that displays the given data.

ch06/jep-fig6-14.cap: Figure 6-14. The LEMAC on this aircraft is at station 860.2 and the TEMAC is at body station number 1,040.9. The mean aerodynamic chord of this wing is 180.7 inches and represents the chord through the center of the wing.

ch06/jep-fig6-15.cap: Figure 6-15. The graph indicates that up to a gross weight of 5,150 pounds, the forward CG limit is +128 inches, and the aft limit is +139.2 inches. However, at the gross weight of 6,725 pounds, the forward limit shifts aft to +134.2 inches while the aft limit remains at +139.2 inches.

ch06/jep-fig6-16.cap: Figure 6-16. (A)— A typical weight and balance chart begins with the aircraft empty weight and moment index. (B)— To use the moment index graph start on the vertical axis with an object's weight. Then move right horizontally until you intersect the proper vertical line. From this intersection, drop down to the bottom of the chart to read the item's moment index.

ch06/jep-fig6-17.cap: Figure 6-17. In this case, draw a horizontal line to the right through the 2,355pound weight and a vertical line up through the 105.5 moment index line. These two lines must intersect within the envelope in order for the aircraft to be loaded properly. In this case, the intersection is within the envelope, near the rearward CG limit.

ch06/jep-fig6-18.cap: Figure 6-18. In a typical manifest, the weight and associated moment indexes are entered into the appropriate spaces. They are then totaled and compared to the aircraft's limits.

ch06/jep-fig6-19.cap: Figure 6-19. To determine if the aircraft is loaded properly, find the weight that matches the aircraft's loaded weight. Since 9,435 pounds is between 9,400 and 9,450 pounds, you must interpolate the minimum and maximum moment index numbers.

ch06/jep-fig6-20.cap: Figure 6-20. To determine how much ballast must be placed at station 170 to move the CG 5 inches aft, use the ballast formula.

ch06/jep-fig6-21.cap: Figure 6-21. It is often helpful to use graphic illustration aids in determining the temporary ballast needed to correct an unusual flight condition. In this example, 58.06 pounds must be carried in the baggage compartment during solo flight from the front seat. Also, always proof the formula by using a typical weight and balance chart.

ch06/jep-fig6-22.cap: Figure 6-22. In order to bring the CG of a large aircraft within the CG range, weight is shifted from one location to another. In this case, the weight is moved from the forward baggage compartment located at station 26 to the aft baggage compartment at station 246.

ch06/jep-fig6-23.cap: Figure 6-23. The empty weight of the airplane is 2,024 pounds and its empty weight CG is +52.5 inches. The radio removed from the instrument panel has a weight of 16 pounds and an arm of +49 inches. The power supply weight is 12 pounds and has an arm of +86. The new radio is installed where the old radio was, but has a weight of +9 pounds. The anticollision beacon weighs +4 pounds and is installed at station +127.

ch06/jep-fig6-24.cap: Figure 6-24. Sample aircraft used for adverse-loaded CG checks.

ch06/jep-fig6-25.cap: Figure 6-25. Once all the items are entered into the chart the total weight and moment are found to be 2,309 pounds and 121,825 pound-inches respectively. This equates to a most forward CG of +52.76 inches.

ch06/jep-fig6-27.cap: Figure 6-27. The maximum gross weight check is accomplished by loading everything with the maximum possible.

ch06/jep-fig6-28.cap: Figure 6-28. On this sample helicopter the datum is located 90.7 inches in front of the nose while one jacking point is located at +151 inches and two others at +290.15 inches.

ch06/jep-fig6-29.cap: Figure 6-29. The leveling procedure used for this helicopter is to hang a plumb bob from the slotted level plate in the baggage compartment. The helicopter is level when the plumb bob is directly over the intersection of the insribed lines.

ch06/jep-fig6-30.cap: Figure 6-30. The empty weight CG of 248.20 falls within the empty weight CG envelope. Therefore no adverse computations are required.

ch06/jep-fig6-31.cap: Figure 6-31. The lateral CG is calculated to be 0.4 inches and the longitudinal CG is 248.20 inches. The intersection of these two CGs falls within the acceptable range.

ch07/jep-fig7-1.cap: Figure 7-1. A material's mass per unit volume is called its density. Water, which is used as a standard, weighs one gram per cubic centimeter and has a density of 1.

ch07/jep-fig7-3.cap: Figure 7-3. Aluminum alloys are heat treated to increase their strength and improve their working characteristics. Heat treatment temperatures and soak times are critical to disperse the alloying elements.

ch07/jep-fig7-4.cap: Figure 7-4. Magnesium alloys use a different designation system than aluminum. For example, the designation AZ31A-T4 identifies an alloy containing 3 percent aluminum and 1 percent zinc that has been solution heat-treated.

ch07/jep-fig7-5.cap: Figure 7-5. This table illustrates the composition, tensile strength, and elongation of titanium alloys. The degree of strength is denoted by the smaller hole elongation percentage shown in the last column. The titanium alloy most commonly used by the aerospace industry is an alpha-beta heat-treated alloy called 6Al-4V. This alloy has a tensile strength of 180 KSI, or 180,000 pounds per square inch. It is frequently used for special fasteners.

ch07/jep-fig7-6.cap: Figure 7-6. The Society of Automotive Engineers has established a classification system for steel alloys. For example, SAE 1030 identifies plain carbon steel containing .30 percent carbon.

ch07/jep-fig7-7.cap: Figure 7-7. To anneal a piece of chrome-molybdenum steel (SAE 4130), it must be heated to between 1,525°F and 1,575° F. This temperature is achieved when the metal is heated to a bright red.

ch07/jep-fig7-8.cap: Figure 7-8. Common tools can be tempered by heating the metal until it turns the proper color, and then quenching.

ch07/jep-fig7-9.cap: Figure 7-9. A Brinell hardness tester determines hardness by forcing a penetrator into a sample and measuring the diameter of the resulting impression.

ch07/jep-fig7-10.cap: Figure 7-10. A Rockwell hardness tester produces the same information as a Brinell tester by measuring the depth of the impression in a sample.

ch07/jep-fig7-11.cap: Figure 7-11. (A) — Quarter-sawing produces a plank more resistant to warpage. (B) — The annual rings of a quarter-sawed plank cross at an angle more than 45 degrees.

ch07/jep-fig7-12.cap: Figure 7-12. This laminated wood propeller is made of thin strips of birch wood glued together, with the grain of all strips running in the same direction.

ch07/jep-fig7-13.cap: Figure 7-13. Modern aircraft construction makes extensive use of plastic materials for engine cowlings, wheel fairings, windshields, and side windows.

ch07/jep-fig7-14.cap: Figure 7-14. When mixed in proper portions, epoxy resins form a high-strength adhesive and provide a good bond between many types of materials.

ch07/jep-fig7-15.cap: Figure 7-15. Phenol-formaldehyde resin is used to impregnate linen cloth to make control cable pulleys. These pulleys have high strength but do not wear the control cable.

ch07/jep-fig7-16.cap: Figure 7-16. Thin filaments, or fibers, of glass are woven into a cloth to reinforce thermosetting resins to form various types of aircraft structures.

ch07/jep-fig7-17.cap: Figure 7-17. A high-strength structural material used to provide an electrically transparent, streamlined housing for radar antennas is made of fiberglass-reinforced honeycomb.

ch07/jep-fig7-18.cap: Figure 7-18. Packing rings are manufactured with different profiles to suit varying operating requirements.

ch07/jep-fig7-19.cap: Figure 7-19. A chevron seal must be installed with the female adapter facing the pressure.

ch07/jep-fig7-20.cap: Figure 7-20. Since a shock absorber cord's elasticity deteriorates with age, a color code indicates its date of manufacture.

ch08/jep-fig8-1.cap: Figure 8-1. Before a rivet is driven, it should extend beyond the base material at least one and a half times the rivet's diameter. Once driven, the rivet shank expands to fill the hole and the bucktail expands to one and a half times its original diameter. Once the bucktail expands to the appropriate diameter it should extend beyond the base material by at least one half the original rivet diameter.

ch08/jep-fig8-2.cap: Figure 8-2. Rivet identification numbers indicate head style, material, and size.

ch08/jep-fig8-4.cap: Figure 8-4. The AN470 rivet now replaces almost all other protruding head designs. The round head rivet (AN430) was used extensively on aircraft built before 1955, while the flat head rivet (AN442) was widely used on internal structures. Flat head rivets are still used for applications requiring higher head strength.

ch08/jep-fig8-6.cap: Figure 8-6. The raised head of a crown flush rivet allows greater contact area with a rivet set. This results in a stronger countersunk joint.

ch08/jep-fig8-7.cap: Figure 8-7. Head markings indicate the alloy used in common aircraft rivets.

ch08/jep-fig8-8.cap: Figure 8-8. Different rivet alloys produce different shear strengths in their driven condition.

ch08/jep-fig8-9.cap: Figure 8-9. POP rivets are frequently used for assembly and non-structural applications. They must not be used in areas that are subject to moderate or heavy loads.

ch08/jep-fig8-10.cap: Figure 8-10. The friction-lock rivet assembly consists of a shell and mandrel or pulling stem. The stem is pulled until the header forms a bucktail on the blind side of the shell. At this point, a weak point built into the stem shears and the stem breaks off. After the stem fractures, part of it projects upward. The projecting stem is cut close to the rivet head and the small residual portion is filed smooth.

ch08/jep-fig8-11.cap: Figure 8-11. Unlike friction lock rivets, HuckLok rivets utilize a lock ring that mechanically locks the center stem in place.

ch08/jep-fig8-12.cap: Figure 8-12. (1) — As the stem is pulled into the rivet sleeve, a bulb forms on the rivet's blind side that begins to clamp the two pieces of metal together and fill the hole. (2) — Once the pieces are clamped tightly together, the bulb continues to form until the shear ring shears and allows the stem to pull further into the rivet. (3) — With the shear ring gone, the stem is pulled upward until the pulling head automatically stops at the stem break notch and the locking collar is ready to be inserted. (4) — When completely installed, the locking collar is inserted and the stem is fractured flush with the rivet head.

ch08/jep-fig8-13.cap: Figure 8-13. (1) — Once an OLYMPIC-LOK rivet is inserted into a prepared hole, the stem is pulled into the sleeve closing any gap between the materials being riveted, filling the hole, and forming a bearing area. (2) — When the stem travel is stopped by the sleeve's internal step, the locking collar shears free and is forced into the locking groove. (3) — Continued pulling breaks the stem flush with the rivet head.

ch08/jep-fig8-14.cap: Figure 8-14. (1) — As the stem pulls into the rivet sleeve it forms a large bulb that seats the rivet head and clamps the two sheets tightly together. (2) — As the blind head is completed, the safe-locking collar moves into the rivet sleeve recess. (3) — As the stem continues to be pulled, the safe-lock collar is formed into the head recess by the driving anvil, locking the stem and sleeve securely together. Further pulling fractures the stem, providing a flush, burr-free installation.

ch08/jep-fig8-17.cap: Figure 8-17. As you can see, both the shear and tension type lockbolts come in a variety of sizes with multiple head styles.

ch08/jep-fig8-18.cap: Figure 8-18. (A) — An allen wrench holds a Hi-Lok bolt in place while a wrench is used to tighten the shear nut. (B) — Once a Hi-Lok is installed, the collar is installed and tightened. When the appropriate torque value is obtained, the wrenching device shears off leaving the collar.

ch08/jep-fig8-19.cap: Figure 8-19. CherryBUCK fasteners combine two titanium alloys to produce a one-piece fastener with 95 KSI shear strength.

ch08/jep-fig8-20.cap: Figure 8-20. The hole fora Taper-Lok is made with a special tapered drill. Once a Taper-Lok is installed and a washer nut is tightened, radial compression forces and vertical compression forces combine to create an extremely strong joint.

ch08/jep-fig8-21.cap: Figure 8-21. This Hi-Tigue features a subtly shaped bead at the threaded end of the shank. This bead preloads the hole it is inserted into thereby strengthening the joint.

ch08/jep-fig8-22.cap: Figure 8-22. Once a Jo-Bolt is inserted into a hole, the bolt is rotated causing the nut to pull up to the metal. As the nut moves upward, a sleeve is forced over the tapered end of the bolt. This creates a blind head that holds the joint together.

ch08/jep-fig8-23.cap: Figure 8-23. Remove flush-type Jo-Bolts by first drilling a pilot hole into the bolt slightly deeper than the inside of the head of the nut. Then, using a drill bit of the same size, drill to the depth of the pilot hole. Drive the shank and blind head from the hole using a pin punch of the proper size.

ch08/jep-fig8-24.cap: Figure 8-24. Rivnuts are commonly available with flat heads and with 100 degree countersunk heads. Countersunk head Rivnuts are made with both 0.048-inch and 0.063-inch head thicknesses, with the thinner head used when it is necessary to install a Rivnut in a machine countersunk hole in thin material. Closed-end Rivnuts are available for installation in a pressurized structure or sealed compartment.

ch08/jep-fig8-25.cap: Figure 8-25. This table indicates fastener diameters, the number of threads per inch, and the bit size required to drill a hole the fastener will fit into or be tapped.

ch08/jep-fig8-26.cap: Figure 8-26. When choosing an AN bolt for a specific application, you must know the diameter, length, and grip length required.

ch08/jep-fig8-27.cap: Figure 8-27. To aid in identifying what type of metal a bolt is made of, bolt heads are marked with a symbol.

ch08/jep-fig8-28.cap: Figure 8-28. To determine the length of an MS20073 or MS20074 drilled-head engine bolt, locate the dash number representing the diameter on the left side of the chart and the dash number representing the length across the top. The intersection of the two dash numbers represents the bolt' 's length. For example, an MS20073-05-12 bolt has fine threads, a diameter of °/,, inch, and a length of 1.297 inches.

ch08/jep-fig8-29.cap: Figure 8-29. Close tolerance bolts carry a triangle mark on their heads and are ground to a much tighter tolerance than standard bolts.

ch08/jep-fig8-30.cap: Figure 8-30. Clevis bolts are loaded in shear only and are frequently used in control cable installations.

ch08/jep-fig8-31.cap: Figure 8-31. High-strength internal wrenching bolts can bear high tension loads and are frequently used to mount engines.

ch08/jep-fig8-32.cap: Figure 8-32. Standard aircraft nuts are available for a variety of applications.

ch08/jep-fig8-33.cap: Figure 8-33. As you can see, there are several different types of self-locking nuts available for multiple applications.

ch08/jep-fig8-34.cap: Figure 8-34. Part codes for self-locking nuts use dash numbers to indicate size and thread pitch. For example, a -524 represents a self-locking nut that fits a 5/16 inch fine thread bolt with 24 threads per inch.

ch08/jep-fig8-35.cap: Figure 8-35. Anchor nuts simplify the process of installing and removing inspection plates. Some of the more familiar anchor nuts are shown above.

ch08/jep-fig8-36.cap: Figure 8-36. To reduce magnetic influences in the cockpit, nonmagnetic mounting nuts secure instruments in a control panel.

ch08/jep-fig8-37.cap: Figure 8-37. Anchor type Tinnerman' nuts are suitable for nonstructural applications.

ch08/jep-fig8-38.cap: Figure 8-38. U-type Tinnerman nuts provide convenient anchor points for cowlings, fairings, and panels.

ch08/jep-fig8-39.cap: Figure 8-39. Manufacturers usually specify torques for threaded fasteners. However, when this information is not available, refer to a standard torque chart.

ch08/jep-fig8-40.cap: Figure 8-40. Machine screws are the most widely used screw in aircraft applications. A variety of sizes and styles are available.

ch08/jep-fig8-41.cap: Figure 8-41. Structural screws are available with both protruding and countersunk heads.

ch08/jep-fig8-42.cap: Figure 8-42. Self-tapping sheet metal screws are useful for attaching trim and upholstery.

ch08/jep-fig8-43.cap: Figure 8-43. MS16562 spring steel rollpins are often used in the movable joints of aircraft seats.

ch08/jep-fig8-45.cap: Figure 8-45. You may use either of the two acceptable methods to safety castellated nuts.

ch08/jep-fig8-46.cap: Figure 8-46. Taper pins produce a tight fit in a reamed hole for applications loaded in shear.

ch08/jep-fig8-47.cap: Figure 8-47. Aircraft washers come in a variety of styles and are used to perform a variety of tasks.

ch08/jep-fig8-50.cap: Figure 8-50. With a standard Dzus fastener, a slotted stud engages a spring mounted to the fuselage. As the stud is turned one quarter turn, the spring locks the fastener in place.

ch08/jep-fig8-51.cap: Figure 8-51. The receptacle of a receptacle-type Dzus fastener guides the stud to the exact location it needs to be prior to engaging the spring.

ch08/jep-fig8-52.cap: Figure 8-52. Airloc cowling fasteners are similar to Dzus fasteners and are used in many of the same applications.

ch08/jep-fig8-53.cap: Figure 8-53. With a Camloc cowling fastener the stud assembly can be inserted into the receptacle when the pin is aligned with the slot in the receptacle.

ch08/jep-fig8-54.cap: Figure 8-54. To check the tension of aircraft control cables a tensiometer is used. To use a tensiometer a cable is placed between the two blocks on the frame and the riser. The trigger is then pulled to apply pressure to the cable and indicate the cable tension.

ch08/jep-fig8-55.cap: Figure 8-55. Different steel control cables are available for various applications based on flexibility and breaking strength.

ch08/jep-fig8-56.cap: Figure 8-56. Swaged cable terminals have all but replaced woven splices and are as strong or stronger than the cable itself.

ch08/jep-fig8-57.cap: Figure 8-57. A go/no-go gauge ensures that a swaged terminal was installed properly.

ch08/jep-fig8-58.cap: Figure 8-58. To install a nicopress sleeve, slip a sleeve over the cable end and loop the cable back through the sleeve. Next, place a proper size AN100 thimble inside the loop, and pull the cable tight leaving about 1/16 inch of cable protruding from the sleeve. Three squeezes are then applied with the squeezing tool. The first squeeze in the middle, the second on the end nearest the thimble, and the last on the sleeve end nearest the free cable end. After the sleeve is squeezed, check it with a gauge to ensure that it has been forced far enough down into the cable.

ch08/jep-fig8-59.cap: Figure 8-59. Turnbuckles provide a means of adjusting control cables as they age and stretch.

ch08/jep-fig8-60.cap: Figure 8-60. Many bolt heads must be safety wired to keep them from vibrating loose. As a general rule, no more than three bolts should be safety wired together.

ch08/jep-fig8-61.cap: Figure 8-61. To prevent nuts from becoming loose on studs, use castellated nuts and safety wire them as you would bolt heads.

ch08/jep-fig8-62.cap: Figure 8-62. Turnbuckles and swaged cable studs must be safetied to prevent them from becoming loose. Of the available methods, double wrapping is preferred.

ch08/jep-fig8-63.cap: Figure 8-63. When safety wiring turnbuckles, make sure you use the proper size safety wire. Brass safety wire can be used on turnbuckles, but a larger size or a double wrap is required to provide the same strength as stainless steel wire.

ch08/jep-fig8-64.cap: Figure 8-64. Locking clips can be used to safety turnbuckles if the barrel and terminal are notched to accept them.

ch08/jep-fig8-65.cap: Figure 8-65. Metric threads utilize letters and numbers to indicate the fastener diameter, the thread pitch, and tolerance classifications.

ch08/jep-fig8-66.cap: Figure 8-66. Metric bolt head markings indicate the strength of the bolt. Underlined bolt markings on 8.8, 9.8, and 10.9 strength bolts indicates the use of a different type of material in fabrication.

ch09/jep-fig9-1.cap: Figure 9-1. A ball peen hammer has a flat face and a ball-shaped end. The flatfaced end should not be used to drive a nail, since the curved face of a claw hammer is better shaped for nail driving control.

ch09/jep-fig9-2.cap: Figure 9-2. (A) — On a cross peen hammer, the wedge is at a right angle to the handle. (B) — On a straight peen hammer, the wedge is parallel to the handle.

ch09/jep-fig9-3.cap: Figure 9-3. There are two types of claw hammers. One type has a curved set of claws that is used for pulling nails, while the other has a straight set of claws that is used to split wood as well as pull nails.

ch09/jep-fig9-5.cap: Figure 9-5. Body hammers do not typically have a great deal of weight to them and are used to smooth metal.

ch09/jep-fig9-6.cap: Figure 9-6. (A) — The rawhide mallet today is used more as a specialized hand tool. (B) — Plastic mallets have virtually replaced rawhide mallets for most uses.

ch09/jep-fig9-7.cap: Figure 9-7. (A) — The end of a punch must have a crowned shape in order to minimize the chance of splitting or chipping. (B) — This illustrates what the end of a punch typically looks like after continuous use.

ch09/jep-fig9-8.cap: Figure 9-8. A punch holder is used when a hard blow is required.

ch09/jep-fig9-9.cap: Figure 9-9. A prick punch is used with a light hammer blow to make reference points on metal.

ch09/jep-fig9-10.cap: Figure 9-10. (A) — A hammer is used with a solid steel center punch to mark sheet metal. (B) — An automatic center punch uses a spring loaded trip mechanism in its handle to create a punch mark.

ch09/jep-fig9-11.cap: Figure 9-11. A pin punch has a flat tip and a uniform shank that is available in several different sizes.

ch09/jep-fig9-12.cap: Figure 9-12. As you can see, a starting punch has a flat face and tapers outward to the shank.

ch09/jep-fig9-13.cap: Figure 9-13. A transfer punch has a shank the same size as the rivet hole being transferred. This way, when it is inserted into an old rivet hole, the new skin is marked for the drill center.

ch09/jep-fig9-14.cap: Figure 9-14. The six-inch slip-joint pliers is the size most commonly used in aircraft maintenance. These pliers get their name from the double hole used for their pivot.

ch09/jep-fig9-15.cap: Figure 9-15. Interlocking-joint pliers have various jaw sizes to allow for a variety of grips.

ch09/jep-fig9-16.cap: Figure 9-16. One thing you must watch for when using VISE-GRIP pliers is that the force applied to the jaws can damage work.

ch09/jep-fig9-17.cap: Figure 9-17. Duckbill pliers are an excellent tool for twisting safety wire because they have serrations that grip the wire and their handles are long enough to provide a tight grip.

ch09/jep-fig9-19.cap: Figure 9-19. Safety wire pliers are used to secure bolt heads or nuts with safety wire.

ch09/jep-fig9-21.cap: Figure 9-21. Cape chisels come in either single-bevel (A), or double-bevel (B), and are typically used to knock off drilled through rivet heads.

ch09/jep-fig9-22.cap: Figure 9-22. The diamond-point chisel gets its name from the shape of its cutting edge.

ch09/jep-fig9-23.cap: Figure 9-23. Parts of a file include the tang, heel, face, edge, and point. A file's laegtisastes syetchoayian ngth fr mtlic heel tothe pole int.

ch09/jep-fig9-24.cap: Figure 9-24. This illustration shows typical single-cut and double-cut files.

ch09/jep-fig9-25.cap: Figure 9-25. Files are classified with regard to their kind, their length, and their cut. The most commonly used files in aviation are the mill file, hand file, halfround file, three-square file, knife file, round file, wood rasp, and the vixen file.

ch09/jep-fig9-26.cap: Figure 9-26. When cross filing, the file is moved lengthwise across the work with hands positioned as illustrated.

ch09/jep-fig9-27.cap: Figure 9-27. In draw filing, the file is moved sideways across the work, with hands positioned as illustrated.

ch09/jep-fig9-28.cap: Figure 9-28. Tin snips make straight or curved cuts.

ch09/jep-fig9-29.cap: Figure 9-29. In addition to being color-coded, aviation snips can be identified by their shape. For example, a straight snip has a relatively straight nose. However, with right-cut snips, when held in your hand, the lower jaw is on the right whereas the lower jaw is on the left with left-cut snips.

ch09/jep-fig9-30.cap: Figure 9-30. Diagonal cutters are commonly used to clip twisted safety wire, and often a version of these cutters are found on needle nose pliers at their pivot point.

ch09/jep-fig9-31.cap: Figure 9-31. The teeth of a crosscut saw act as knives to cut through wood fibers. The kerf of the teeth dictates the width of the cut.

ch09/jep-fig9-33.cap: Figure 9-33. Backsaws cut very straight and are therefore used for cutting precision parts.

ch09/jep-fig9-34.cap: Figure 9-34. A keyhole saw has a thin tapered blade that allows a large hole to be cut when only a small hole exists.

ch09/jep-fig9-35.cap: Figure 9-35. When choosing a hacksaw blade you should select one that allows at least two teeth to rest on the work at all times.

ch09/jep-fig9-36.cap: Figure 9-36. (A) — The auger bit is designed to drill holes through a material. (B) — The Forstner bit, on the other hand, is designed to drill flat-bottomed holes.

ch09/jep-fig9-37.cap: Figure 9-37. A tapered pilot ona flat wooden boring bit aids in keeping the cutting edges centered in the hole.

ch09/jep-fig9-38.cap: Figure 9-38. On a typical metal drill, the cutting edges on the point perform the actual cutting. The lands and flutes remove the cut material and carry lubricant to the cutting edges.

ch09/jep-fig9-39.cap: Figure 9-39. Grinding the point of a drill is complicated because of the many angles involved. Because of this, it is best to use a grinding fixture whenever possible.

ch09/jep-fig9-40.cap: Figure 9-40. Drill sizes are given by number, in fractional form, by letter, and in millimeters.

ch09/jep-fig9-42.cap: Figure 9-42. In the drill speed chart above, you can see the relationship between hole size, drill speed, and the type of material used.

ch09/jep-fig9-43.cap: Figure 9-43. Prior to using a hole saw you need to mark the center of the hole so you know where to start the pilot bit.

ch09/jep-fig9-45.cap: Figure 9-45. Stop countersinks are used to recess a rivet head flush with the material being riveted.

ch09/jep-fig9-46.cap: Figure 9-46. With a solid reamer such as the tapered reamer and bottoming reamer only one size hole can be cut. However, with an expansion reamer several different size holes can be cut with the same reamer.

ch09/jep-fig9-47.cap: Figure 9-47. A typical chart shows both the body drill and the tap drill sizes for standard screw threads from size 0-80 up through one inch.

ch09/jep-fig9-48.cap: Figure 9-48. Measurements on the metric tap charts are given in millimeters.

ch09/jep-fig9-50.cap: Figure 9-50. When using either the T-handle or the solid handle to turn a tap, make sure to apply even pressure to both sides of the handle.

ch09/jep-fig9-52.cap: Figure 9-52. Screwdrivers are available with several shank lengths ranging from 1 1/2 inches to about 12 inches. However, some special-purpose screwdrivers may have a shank length of 20 inches and more.

ch09/jep-fig9-53.cap: Figure 9-53. An offset screwdriver like the one shown here allows screws to be removed and tightened when there is no clearance for a straight screwdriver.

ch09/jep-fig9-54.cap: Figure 9-54. A screwdriver with replaceable bits is a very handy tool for aircraft maintenance technicians working away from their tool boxes.

ch09/jep-fig9-55.cap: Figure 9-55. Prior to using an air-driven screwdriver you should make sure you understand how to set the proper torque.

ch09/jep-fig9-57.cap: Figure 9-57. The end of a screwdriver blade should be ground flat and fill approximately 75 percent of the screw slot width.

ch09/jep-fig9-58.cap: Figure 9-58. A Phillips head screwdriver has a relatively blunt point that fits into a flat-bottomed hole.

ch09/jep-fig9-60.cap: Figure 9-60. The TRI-WING screw and bit have three wings instead of a straight slot or cross shaped tip.

ch09/jep-fig9-62.cap: Figure 9-62. Although most of the fasteners used on aircraft are in English sizes, you may come across some metric hardware. The above is a chart of the most common sizes found.

ch09/jep-fig9-63.cap: Figure 9-63. Wrench sizes are measured across the flats of bolt heads and nuts …

ch09/jep-fig9-64.cap: Figure 9-64. The end of an open-end wrench is typically attached at a 15 degree angle. However, on some wrenches the head is attached at a 30 to 60 degree angle.

ch09/jep-fig9-65.cap: Figure 9-65. Because of their enclosed design, box-end wrenches are less likely to slip.

ch09/jep-fig9-66.cap: Figure 9-66. Combination wrenches have the advantages of a box-end and an open-end.

ch09/jep-fig9-67.cap: Figure 9-67. Since a flare nut wrench can engage a nut every 15 degrees of handle movement, it is ideal for use in confined areas.

ch09/jep-fig9-68.cap: Figure 9-68. A ratcheting open-end wrench is left open on one end to allow a ratcheting action.

ch09/jep-fig9-69.cap: Figure 9-69. Most ratcheting box-end wrenches are locked in one direction, thus to change the direction of movement, the wrench is turned over.

ch09/jep-fig9-70.cap: Figure 9-70. Standard sockets are available with four, six, eight, and 12 point openings.

ch09/jep-fig9-71.cap: Figure 9-71. Deep sockets aid in the removal of items such as spark plugs.

ch09/jep-fig9-72.cap: Figure 9-72. Flex sockets have a pivot point that allows for more flexibility.

ch09/jep-fig9-73.cap: Figure 9-73. Crowsfoot sockets are used in locations where a box-end, open-end, or standard socket wrench cannot be used.

ch09/jep-fig9-74.cap: Figure 9-74. Most 3/8 inch ratchet handles are approximately 10 inches in length and their ratcheting action is reversible.

ch09/jep-fig9-75.cap: Figure 9-75. Ratchet adapters fit onto nonratcheting drives and extensions to convert them into a ratcheting wrench.

ch09/jep-fig9-77.cap: Figure 9-77. Speed handles allow screws and nuts to be turned much faster than when using a conventional screwdriver or ratchet.

ch09/jep-fig9-80.cap: Figure 9-80. Exercise discretion when using adapters since the added force exerted has the potential to break either the adaptor or the socket, or strip threads on a fastener.

ch09/jep-fig9-81.cap: Figure 9-81. A hand-held impact driver and hammer are used to loosen corroded fasteners.

ch09/jep-fig9-82.cap: Figure 9-82. The torque produced by a power impact tool is applied in a series of blows or spikes of torque. For this reason, impact wrenches cannot be used on fasteners where torque is critical.

ch09/jep-fig9-83.cap: Figure 9-83. The torque measured by a torque wrench is the product of the length between the drive square and the point of force on the handle.

ch09/jep-fig9-84.cap: Figure 9-84. A torsion bar-type torque wrench uses deflection as well as a bending force to indicate torque.

ch09/jep-fig9-85.cap: Figure 9-85. A toggle torque wrench releases or snaps over when a pre-set torque is reached.

ch09/jep-fig9-87.cap: Figure 9-87. The actual amount of torque applied to a fastener when a five inch extension is used with 120 pounds of indicated torque is 150 inch-pounds.

ch09/jep-fig9-88.cap: Figure 9-88. Most torque values are provided by the manufacturer. However, if a value isn't provided, a table of torque values is used.

ch09/jep-fig9-90.cap: Figure 9-90. These torque guidelines do not replace manufacturer provided torque values.

ch09/jep-fig9-91.cap: Figure 9-91. The proper use of a steel scale requires that the end of the scale not be used to make a measurement. Instead, the one inch mark is used as the starting point. However, you must remember to subtract one inch from the final measurement.

ch09/jep-fig9-92.cap: Figure 9-92. Ascribe is typically used with layout dye to mark reference points on a material. However, scribe marks should never be used for bend lines as they cause stress concentrations that can lead to component failure.

ch09/jep-fig9-93.cap: Figure 9-93. The combination set typically includes a center head, a protractor head, and a stock head. The stock head usually has a level and a scribe built into it.

ch09/jep-fig9-94.cap: Figure 9-94. A divider is used to lay out circles and arcs on your work.

ch09/jep-fig9-95.cap: Figure 9-95. Thickness gauges allow quick measurement of the clearance between two surfaces.

ch09/jep-fig9-96.cap: Figure 9-96. Inside calipers have legs with ends that curve to the outside, whereas outside calipers have legs with ends that curve to the inside.

ch09/jep-fig9-97.cap: Figure 9-97. Hermaphrodite calipers are used to mark distances away from edges. These calipers have the straight leg of a divider and a leg that curves inward similar to an outside caliper.

ch09/jep-fig9-98.cap: Figure 9-98. Attached to the bottom of the frame is the anvil, while the spindle is attached to the top of the frame. The sleeve covers the spindle body and is marked in increments of .025 inch. The thimble spins around the spindle and sleeve and is used to adjust the distance between the anvil and spindle.

ch09/jep-fig9-99.cap: Figure 9-99. Each mark on the sleeve of the micrometer caliper represents 0.025 inch.

ch09/jep-fig9-100.cap: Figure 9-100. (A) — This micrometer shows no marks on the sleeve and the zero line on the thimble in line with the reference line on the sleeve. When set this way, the spindle and anvil should be touching. (B) — The thimble on this micrometer has moved out 0.001 inch and the zero mark on the sleeve is just visible. (C) — There are four lines visible on this micrometer indicating the thimble has moved out at least 0.100 inch. The thimble has also moved out another complete revolution or 0.025 inch. When added together, the thimble has moved out 0.125 inch. (D) —There are seven lines visible on the sleeve indicating the thimble has moved out at least 0.175 inch. The 12 on the thimble is lined up with the reference line on the sleeve indicating the thimble has moved out an additional 0.012 inch. When added together, the thimble has moved out 0.187 inch.

ch09/jep-fig9-101.cap: Figure 9-101. Micrometer calipers for measuring between one and two inches have a one-inch space between the anvil and the spindle when the micrometer reads zero.

ch09/jep-fig9-102.cap: Figure 9-102. A micrometer caliper is calibrated by carefully rotating the sleeve until its longitudinal line exactly aligns with the zero mark on the thimble.

ch09/jep-fig9-103.cap: Figure 9-103. Each mark on the sleeve represents 0.50 millimeters.

ch09/jep-fig9-104.cap: Figure 9-104. (A) - The thimble on this micrometer has moved out 4.0 mm. The 30 on the thimble is lined up with the reference line on the sleeve indicating the thimble has moved out an additional 0.30 mm. Added together, the thimble has moved out 4.30 mm. (B) - The thimble on this micrometer has moved out 7.5 mm. The 48 on the thimble is lined up with the reference line on the sleeve indicating the thimble has moved out an additional 0.48 mm. Added together, the thimble has moved out 7.98 mm.

ch09/jep-fig9-105.cap: Figure 9-105. (A) The sleeve indicates a measurement of at least 0.275 inch. The thimble indicates an additional 0.020 inch. On the vernier scale, the line representing 0.0004 lines up with an increment on the thimble and, therefore, is added to the measurement. The total measurement is 0.2954 (0.275 + 0.020 + 0.0004 = 0.2954). (B) The sleeve indicates a measurement of at least 4.0 mm and the thimble shows an additional 0.36 mm. On the vernier scale, the horizontal line representing 0.002 lines up with an increment on the thimble and, therefore, is added to the total measurement. The resulting dimension is 4.362 mm (4.0 + 0.36 + 0.002 = 4,362).

ch09/jep-fig9-106.cap: Figure 9-106. Inside micrometers use a standard micrometer caliper and various extensions to obtain the inside diameters and widths of slots.

ch09/jep-fig9-107.cap: Figure 9-107. To allow micrometer depth gauges to measure several different grooves, recesses, and bores, most have interchangeable spindles of various lengths.

ch09/jep-fig9-108.cap: Figure 9-108. A vernier caliper consists of a bar scale with one fixed jaw and one movable jaw. The movable jaw typically has a clamp to lock the jaw in place, as well as an adjustment screw for making small jaw movements.

ch09/jep-fig9-110.cap: Figure 9-110. By referencing the zero indication on the 20-division metric vernier scale, you can see that the dimension is larger than 30 mm. By looking down the vernier scale you can also see that only the 75 is alinged with the bar scale. Therefore, 0.75 must be added to the final dimension. The total is 30.75 mm or 3.075 cm.

ch09/jep-fig9-111.cap: Figure 9-111. Dial indicators are used to check shafts for out-of-round and for bends, and they are also useful for checking backlash in gears and for measuring axle end play.

ch09/jep-fig9-112.cap: Figure 9-112. Small hole gauges that measure inside diameters range from 1/8 to 1/2 inch. Telescoping gauges are used for measuring the inside diameter of holes that range from 3/16 to six inches. Both are used in conjunction with a micrometer caliper.

ch10/jep-fig10-1.cap: Figure 10-1. Small-diameter aluminum tubing carries a color code to indicate its alloy.

ch10/jep-fig10-2.cap: Figure 10-2. Magnet and acid tests help identify various ferrous alloys.

ch10/jep-fig10-3.cap: Figure 10-3. To use a tube cutter, gradually increase pressure on the cutting wheel while rotating the cutter toward its open side.

ch10/jep-fig10-4.cap: Figure 10-4. An acceptable bend maintains at least 75 percent of the original tube outside diameter and is free of wrinkles and kinks.

ch10/jep-fig10-5.cap: Figure 10-5. To avoid making bad tubing bends, refer toa chart for standard bend radii.

ch10/jep-fig10-6.cap: Figure 10-6. Use a hand-held tubing bender to form tubing 1/2 inch or smaller in diameter.

ch10/jep-fig10-7.cap: Figure 10-7. A production-type tube bender is used to bend tubing larger than 1/2 inch in diameter.

ch10/jep-fig10-8.cap: Figure 10-8. The combination of an AN 818 nut and AN 819 sleeve provides a tight, leak-free attachment that does not damage the flare.

ch10/jep-fig10-9.cap: Figure 10-9. Singleand double-flared ends are used on rigid tubing.

ch10/jep-fig10-10.cap: Figure 10-10. With an impact-type flaring tool, the tubing is clamped in flaring blocks while the plunger is driven into the tube to produce the flare.

ch10/jep-fig10-11.cap: Figure 10-11. With a roll-type flaring tool the flaring cone is turned into the tube eliminating the need for hammering.

ch10/jep-fig10-12.cap: Figure 10-12. To prevent leakage, be sure that single flares fall within proper dimensional tolerances.

ch10/jep-fig10-13.cap: Figure 10-13. Double flaring a rigid tube produces a stronger flare that is more resistant to leakage.

ch10/jep-fig10-14.cap: Figure 10-14. As with single flares, proper dimensional tolerances must be observed for double flares to produce a leak-free seal.

ch10/jep-fig10-15.cap: Figure 10-15. In addition to the differences mentioned, there are also differences in the flare angle, the type of threads, the body length, and the fitting color.

ch10/jep-fig10-16.cap: Figure 10-16. AN fittings are available in many shapes and sizes to suit a variety of installation requirements.

ch10/jep-fig10-17.cap: Figure 10-17. Pipe fittings use tapered threads to provide a seal. They are not interchangeable with AN fittings.

ch10/jep-fig10-18.cap: Figure 10-18. Flareless fittings must be preset before assembly to provide a tight seal. A properly preset fitting produces a slight, uniform indentation in the rigid tube, whereas, excessive presetting cuts deeply into the tube and weakens it.

ch10/jep-fig10-19.cap: Figure 10-19. Tube beading provides a convenient sealing method for low-pressure applications.

ch10/jep-fig10-20.cap: Figure 10-20. If hose clamps are tightened excessively, the hose "cold flows" through the clamp and becomes susceptible to leakage. It is also important that the beaded tubes are not offset or misaligned.

ch10/jep-fig10-21.cap: Figure 10-21. The amount of torque applied to a fitting varies with the type of tubing and the fitting size.

ch10/jep-fig10-22.cap: Figure 10-22. When a manufacturer does not specify torques for flareless fittings, a table of standard torque values should be used.

ch10/jep-fig10-23.cap: Figure 10-23. To help absorb the stress caused by vibration, tubing should have at least one bend.

ch10/jep-fig10-25.cap: Figure 10-25. The most commonly used types of clamps for aircraft are the rubber cushioned clamp and the plain clamp.

ch10/jep-fig10-26.cap: Figure 10-26. One way to remove small dents in metal tubing is to draw a small metal slug, or bullet, through a tube.

ch10/jep-fig10-27.cap: Figure 10-27. Remove damaged tubing and replace it with a new piece of tubing. The cut ends are flared and connected with standard hardware.

ch10/jep-fig10-28.cap: Figure 10-28. Color codes identify the fluid a line carries and warn of potential hazards.

ch10/jep-fig10-29.cap: Figure 10-29. A lay line shows if a hose is twisted when it is installed.

ch10/jep-fig10-30.cap: Figure 10-30. The maximum operating pressure of low pressure hose varies with the size.

ch10/jep-fig10-31.cap: Figure 10-31. Depending on diameter, medium-pressure hose can carry up to 3,000 psi.

ch10/jep-fig10-33.cap: Figure 10-33. Swaged fittings require special machinery for assembly and cannot be reused.

ch10/jep-fig10-34.cap: Figure 10-34. The reusable fitting can be removed and installed with basic hand tools in the shop.

ch10/jep-fig10-35.cap: Figure 10-35. To ensure that the final assembly is the correct length, use the old hose as a pattern.

ch10/jep-fig10-36.cap: Figure 10-36. Flexible hose fabrication consists of four basic steps. (A) — With the socket held in a vise, screw the hose into the socket. (B) — Next, lubricate the assembly tool and force it into the hose to open the inner liner. (C) — The nipple is then screwed into the socket with the assembly tool. (D) — Once installed, there should be approximately 1/32 to 1/16 inch clearance between the nut and socket to allow the nut to turn freely.

ch10/jep-fig10-37.cap: Figure 10-37. Never install a flexible hose tightly between two fittings. Always ensure there is enough slack in the installation to allow for expansion and contraction.

ch11/jep-fig11-1.cap: Figure 11-1. A special flashlight with an extension for the bulb allows inspection of hard-to-reach locations.

ch11/jep-fig11-2.cap: Figure 11-2. A borescope allows inspection of internal engine components without disassembling the engine.

ch11/jep-fig11-3.cap: Figure 11-3. A fiberoptic borescope uses the principle of light transmission through flexible glass fibers to see inside inaccessible areas.

ch11/jep-fig11-4.cap: Figure 11-4. With a video scope, light is carried to an object by fiberoptics or lightemitting diodes. The image is viewed through a lens by a light sensitive chip and transmitted to a video processor where the electronic signal from the chip is assembled and output to a monitor. Images can be recorded and saved utilizing a variety of data storage technologies including DVD, VHS, and memory cards, or uploaded directly to a computer.

ch11/jep-fig11-5.cap: Figure 11-5. (A) — The most common welds encountered in aviation are the butt weld, double butt weld, lap weld, fillet weld, and edge weld. (B) — A good weld tapers evenly into the base metal and shows good penetration free of gas pockets.

ch11/jep-fig11-6.cap: Figure 11-6. Proper penetration is the single most important characteristic of a good weld.

ch11/jep-fig11-7.cap: Figure 11-7. (A) — Excessive heat causes pitting and a pointed appearance on the ripples. (B) — Insufficient heat causes a weld with rough, irregular edges that are not feathered into the base metal. Penetration is poor. (C) — Too much acetylene produces a weld with craters along the edges. (D) — A cold weld displays irregular edges and considerable variation in the depth of penetration.

ch11/jep-fig11-8.cap: Figure 11-8. (A) — When performing a liquid penetrant inspection, the penetrant is spread over the surface of the material being examined, and allowed sufficient time for capillary action to take place. (B) — The excess penetrant is then washed from the surface, leaving any cracks and surface flaws filled. (C) — An absorbent developer is sprayed over the surface where it blots out any penetrant. The crack then shows up as a bright line against the white developer.

ch11/jep-fig11-9.cap: Figure 11-9. (A) left — Colored dye is used in this penetrating liquid so that examination under white light can be accomplished. (B) right— A fluorescent dye is used in this penetrant inspection and then the part is examined under black or ultraviolet light where any fault appears as a vivid green mark.

ch11/jep-fig11-10.cap: Figure 11-10. Spray cans of cleaner, penetrant, and developer make dye penetrant inspection an effective and handy method of field inspection. However, large parts inspected by dye penetrant are typically dipped in vats of penetrant.

ch11/jep-fig11-12.cap: Figure 11-12. When a part is magnetized in a coil, or solenoid, the lines of flux pass through the material longitudinally. The same holds true if a part is magnetized using a coil wrapped around a soft iron yoke. In both cases, as the flux lines pass through the part longitudinally, faults that run across the part are detected.

ch11/jep-fig11-13.cap: Figure 11-13. When current passes through a part, lines of flux encircle the part making it circularly magnetized. The same holds true when a circular or tubular part is placed over a current-carrying conductor. This circular magnetization allows for the detection of faults extending lengthwise along the part.

ch11/jep-fig11-14.cap: Figure 11-14. Current flowing through a flat object from high-current probes magnetizes the part circularly and detects cracks or faults that are in line with the probes.

ch11/jep-fig11-15.cap: Figure 11-15. Hand shakers, spray bulbs, or powder guns are typically used to apply dry iron oxides.

ch11/jep-fig11-16.cap: Figure 11-16. This propeller blade was magnetized and is being inspected by the residual method.

ch11/jep-fig11-17.cap: Figure 11-17. This crankshaft is magnetized by flowing current through the two heads of the magnetizing machine. Oxide is suspended ina light oil and is flowed over the magnetized part to inspect it.

ch11/jep-fig11-18.cap: Figure 11-18. The fatigue crack in this landing gear outer cylinder changes direction, is jagged and should not be confused with a seam.

ch11/jep-fig11-19.cap: Figure 11-19. The heat-treat cracks on cylinder barrel walls typically have very heavy patterns.

ch11/jep-fig11-20.cap: Figure 11-20. The types of defects found on a test bar are indicative of what you could find on an object being tested.

ch11/jep-fig11-21.cap: Figure 11-21. The eddy current probe is being zeroed by placing it inside a piece of material with the same characteristics as the propeller blade to be inspected.

ch11/jep-fig11-22.cap: Figure 11-22. The absolute method of eddy current inspection measures the amount of current required to induce a given amount of eddy current into the test specimen.

ch11/jep-fig11-23.cap: Figure 11-23. The comparison method of eddy current inspection compares the eddy current induced into a reference material with the eddy current flowing in the material being tested.

ch11/jep-fig11-24.cap: Figure 11-24. Eddy current instruments with a two-dimensional display indicate the presence of a crack as stretched loops.

ch11/jep-fig11-25.cap: Figure 11-25. Generation of ultrasonic vibration is created by piezoelectric materials that physically distort when subjected to an electrical potential.

ch11/jep-fig11-26.cap: Figure 11-26. An oscillator generates AC energy which is amplified and sent to a transducer that creates mechanical vibrations within the material.

ch11/jep-fig11-27.cap: Figure 11-27. (A) — The ultrasonic transducer is mounted on an acrylic adapter and then it beams ultrasonic wave energy into the material being tested. (B) — The transducer is adjusted with reference material before use.

ch11/jep-fig11-28.cap: Figure 11-28. (A) — Vibrations are passed through a material and bounce off of its back surface. (B) — A peak is recorded on the base line to represent both the front and back surfaces.

ch11/jep-fig11-29.cap: Figure 11-29. Ultrasonic energy bounces off a fault and is reflected on the CRT screen as a peak on the base line between the peaks representing the front and back surfaces.

ch11/jep-fig11-30.cap: Figure 11-30. X-rays are produced when electrons from the cathode bombard the target anode and dislodge electrons.

ch11/jep-fig11-32.cap: Figure 11-32. Radiation from x-rays or gamma rays penetrates a specimen and exposes a photographic film. The denser the material, the less the film is exposed.

ch11/jep-fig11-33.cap: Figure 11-33. If a permanent record is not required, a fluoroscope can give a lowresolution image of a part's interior. The materials viewed on a fluorescent screen give an indication similar to those seen on x-ray film.

ch11/jep-fig11-34.cap: Figure 11-34. Portable ultrasonic inspection equipment enables technicians to inspect composite structures and detect damage.

ch12/jep-fig12-1.cap: Figure 12-1. Wheel wells accumulate deposits of dirt, oil, and hydraulic fluid. An emulsifying cleaner should be sprayed into the wheel well and allowed to soak, then washed off with water.

ch12/jep-fig12-2.cap: Figure 12-2. The metals listed above are arranged in order of electrode potential. Any metal appearing in this series is anodic to any metal which follows it and will corrode if subjected to galvanic action.

ch12/jep-fig12-3.cap: Figure 12-3. A simple battery explains the formation of corrosion, as electrons leaving the anode attract chlorine ions from the electrolyte to form aluminum chloride, which is the visible evidence of corrosion.

ch12/jep-fig12-4.cap: Figure 12-4. Aluminum alloys have both anodic and cathodic areas. Corrosion appears at the anodic area when chlorine atoms from the electrolyte join the aluminum chloride.

ch12/jep-fig12-5.cap: Figure 12-5. Iron oxide, more commonly known as rust, forms a porous scale on the surface of a material. Therefore, it will continue to convert the iron oxide as long as it remains on the surface.

ch12/jep-fig12-6.cap: Figure 12-6. Pitting corrosion forms clumps of powdery salts of corrosion on the surface of the metal as it is corroded.

ch12/jep-fig12-7.cap: Figure 12-7. This photomicrograph of the surface of an aluminum sheet shows pitting that is a result of corrosion.

ch12/jep-fig12-8.cap: Figure 12-8. A potential for galvanic corrosion exists when a steel fastener is used to hold a 2024 aluminum alloy inspection plate in place. If contaminated moisture gets between the two metals, the aluminum is corroded rather than the steel screw. However, if 2024 aluminum alloy and magnesium are riveted together and covered by an electrolyte, the magnesium corrodes instead of the aluminum.

ch12/jep-fig12-9.cap: Figure 12-9. Oxygen concentration cell corrosion forms in the areas where there is a deficiency of oxygen.

ch12/jep-fig12-11.cap: Figure 12-11. Metallic ion concentration cell corrosion forms in the open at the edge of the lap joint.

ch12/jep-fig12-12.cap: Figure 12-12. Filiform corrosion forms under the dense film of a polyurethane finish, where it first appears as a puffiness under the finish.

ch12/jep-fig12-13.cap: Figure 12-13. Intergranular corrosion of 7075-16 aluminum adjacent to a steel fastener. The electrolyte needed for this action is supplied from the surface through corrosion deposits, and the attack continues along the grain boundaries.

ch12/jep-fig12-14.cap: Figure 12-14. The water marks on this hardened steel bearing race are indications of intergranular corrosion in the hardened metal.

ch12/jep-fig12-16.cap: Figure 12-16. Stress corrosion forms at the end of a crack and rapidly enlarges the crack until the material fails.

ch12/jep-fig12-17.cap: Figure 12-17. Fretting corrosion causes black residue to trail out behind the rivet, causing it to appear to smoke.

ch12/jep-fig12-18.cap: Figure 12-18. Microbial growth within a turbine aircraft fuel tank forms a scum that holds water against the metal and causes corrosion to form.

ch12/jep-fig12-19.cap: Figure 12-19. The strong acid or alkaline fumes around a battery box can cause corrosion on the adjacent structure.

ch12/jep-fig12-20.cap: Figure 12-20. The food service area in an aircraft is subject to corrosion damage if spilled food traps water against the structure where it cannot be removed.

ch12/jep-fig12-21.cap: Figure 12-21. Wheel wells are corrosion-prone areas because abrasion from water and dirt removes the protective finish, and dirt and grease can trap and hold moisture against the aluminum.

ch12/jep-fig12-22.cap: Figure 12-22. Wheel well and landing gear corrosion points.

ch12/jep-fig12-23.cap: Figure 12-23. Corrosion in a spot-welded seam can be detected by laying a straightedge over the seam. Corrosion causes the seam to have a wavy surface.

ch12/jep-fig12-24.cap: Figure 12-24. A piano hinge must be kept dry and free from dirt which could cause galvanic corrosion because of the different metals used in the hinge.

ch12/jep-fig12-26.cap: Figure 12-26. The drain holes in the bottom of a structure must be kept open to prevent moisture from collecting and causing corrosion.

ch12/jep-fig12-27.cap: Figure 12-27. The landing gear box is one of the most highly stressed areas in an aircraft structure, and is one of the least accesible for adequate inspection.

ch12/jep-fig12-28.cap: Figure 12-28. A steel control cable must be carefully inspected to be sure there is no corrosion in the strands. If there is any sign of corrosion, the cable must be replaced.

ch12/jep-fig12-29.cap: Figure 12-29. Surface preparation is the most critical phase of aircraft refinishing. Cleaning and paint stripping must be performed properly to produce a quality finish.

ch12/jep-fig12-30.cap: Figure 12-30. Typical corrosion removal and treatment procedures for aluminum alloys.

ch12/jep-fig12-32.cap: Figure 12-32. Clean the area around corrosion pits to a width that is 10 times the depth of the corrosion, and a length that is 20 times the depth of corrosion. This ensures that all traces of corrosion are eliminated.

ch12/jep-fig12-33.cap: Figure 12-33. This chart lists the metal combinations requiring a protective separator. The separating materials can be metal primer, aluminum tape, washers, grease, or sealant, depending on the metals involved.

ch12/jep-fig12-34.cap: Figure 12-34. Fuel tanks are sealed with a special resilient sealer in all of the seams.

ch13/jep-fig13-2.cap: Figure 13-2. Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) provide information on hazardous materials that are present in the workplace. Furthermore, all employers must maintain current copies of all Material Safety Data Sheets for reference at any time.

ch13/jep-fig13-3.cap: Figure 13-3. The material described by this sample hazard label presents a serious flammability hazard (red), a moderate hazard to health (blue), and a minimum stability hazard (yellow). When handling this material, the use of goggles, gloves and respirator (G) is required for personal protection.

ch13/jep-fig13-5.cap: Figure 13-5. Be sure the eye-protection shields are in place when using a bench grinder.

ch13/jep-fig13-6.cap: Figure 13-6. Face shields or goggles should be used when drilling, grinding, or sawing.

ch13/jep-fig13-7.cap: Figure 13-7. Be sure that all fire extinguishers are properly serviced, and are clearly marked to indicate the type of fire they are suited for.

ch13/jep-fig13-8.cap: Figure 13-8. Fires are divided into four classes to allow selection of the proper extinguishing agent.

ch13/jep-fig13-9.cap: Figure 13-9. Halogenated hydrocarbon fire extinguishers provide effective fire suppression in aircraft engine compartments.

ch13/jep-fig13-10.cap: Figure 13-10. A dry-powder fire extinguisher blankets a fire to exclude oxygen from the fuel.

ch13/jep-fig13-11.cap: Figure 13-11. The content of the propellant of a dry-powder extinguisher is indicated by the pressure gauge.

ch13/jep-fig13-12.cap: Figure 13-12. Aircraft manufacturers provide jack pads on landing gear to allow jacking one wheel at a time.

ch13/jep-fig13-13.cap: Figure 13-13. Ajack's safety collar should be used to keep the jack from collapsing if a seal fails.

ch13/jep-fig13-14.cap: Figure 13-14. Be sure to follow the aircraft manufacturer's recommendations when hoisting an aircraft.

ch13/jep-fig13-15.cap: Figure 13-15. The high noise levels encountered in aircraft operation areas can seriously damage your hearing. Hearing protectors such as these can prevent hearing loss.

ch13/jep-fig13-16.cap: Figure 13-16. When you are in the vicinity of jet aircraft that are running their engines, stay clear of the danger areas shown.

ch13/jep-fig13-17.cap: Figure 13-17. Illustrated are some of the more commonly accepted safety practices to use around helicopters.

ch13/jep-fig13-18.cap: Figure 13-18. Control battens are used to securely lock an aircraft's control surfaces in place. They should have red streamers attached to help prevent their inadvertently being left on the aircraft when it is prepared for flight.

ch13/jep-fig13-19.cap: Figure 13-19. If an airplane must be left outside in a windstorm, spoilers can be lashed to the top of the wing to prevent generation of lift.

ch13/jep-fig13-20.cap: Figure 13-20. When securing an aircraft on a crowded ramp, observe the minimum clearances shown in this diagram.

ch13/jep-fig13-21.cap: Figure 13-21. The bowline is the most generally used knot for tying an aircraft with ropes.

ch13/jep-fig13-24.cap: Figure 13-24. In addition to securing a helicopter to the ground, you must also secure the helicopter's rotor blades to its fuselage.

ch13/jep-fig13-25.cap: Figure 13-25. It is important that the person starting a turbine engine be thoroughly familiar with the procedure.

ch13/jep-fig13-26.cap: Figure 13-26. Standard hand signals allow ground personnel to direct the movement of aircraft.

ch13/jep-fig13-27.cap: Figure 13-27. Located in the cab of the control tower is a powerful light that controllers can use to direct light beams of various colors toward you aircraft. Each color or color combination has a specific meaning for an aircraft on the airport surface.

ch13/jep-fig13-28.cap: Figure 13-28. When towing an aircraft, be sure that the limits of nose wheel movement are observed since the towing stops can be damaged if these limits are exceeded.

ch13/jep-fig13-29.cap: Figure 13-29. The attachment of small wheels to the skids allows for easier ground handling on most light helicopters.

ch13/jep-fig13-30.cap: Figure 13-30. A hydraulic power unit replaces the engine-driven pump to produce hydraulic pressure for gear retraction tests.

ch13/jep-fig13-31.cap: Figure 13-31. This chart illustrates the pressure created in a cylinder as it passes through its various strokes. As you can see, when normal combustion occurs, cylinder pressure builds and dissipates evenly. However, when detonation occurs, cylinder pressure fluctuates dramatically.

ch13/jep-fig13-32.cap: Figure 13-32. This illustration depicts the colors of the various grades and types of aviation fuels as well as the markings and color codes used on fuel conduits and controls.

ch13/jep-fig13-33.cap: Figure 13-33. Before opening the fuel tanks or connecting the fuel hose, be sure that the aircraft and the fuel truck are connected together by an electrical bonding cable.

ch13/jep-fig13-34.cap: Figure 13-34. A biocidal agent is added to turbine fuel to prevent microbial growths that cause corrosion in the fuel tanks.

ch13/jep-fig13-35.cap: Figure 13-35. An aircraft fuel tank must be clearly marked with the proper grade of fuel required.

ch13/jep-fig13-36.cap: Figure 13-36. High rates of fuel flow can be put into an aircraft system from the underwing fueling ports.

ch14/jep-fig14-1.cap: Figure 14-1. The FAA issues Advisory Circulars to explain or clarify the Federal Aviation Regulations. Advisory Circulars are nonregulatory in nature unless incorporated into an FAR and generally do not contain approved data.

ch14/jep-fig14-2.cap: Figure 14-2. A Type Certificate Data Sheet is issued to an aircraft when the FAA approves its design. The TCDS contains important information for use in aircraft maintenance.

ch14/jep-fig14-4.cap: Figure 14-4. Wireless networks and handheld devices make maintenance documents and aircraft records portable.

ch14/jep-fig14-5.cap: Figure 14-5. When performing an inspection, you must use a checklist that follows the requirements of FAR Part 43, Appendix D.

ch14/jep-fig14-6.cap: Figure 14-6. An FAA Form 337 is used to document major repairs and alterations to airframes, powerplants, propellers, and appliances.

ch14/jep-fig14-7.cap: Figure 14-7. Aviation maintenance technicians perform a valuable service by using FAA Form 8010-4 Malfunction or Defect Reports. This voluntary program gathers information on general aviation maintenance problems.

ch14/jep-fig14-8.cap: Figure 14-8. A Standard Airworthiness Certificate is issued to an aircraft and must remain on the aircraft during operation.

ch14/jep-fig14-9.cap: Figure 14-9. A Certificate of Aircraft Registration is issued to an aircraft owner when the aircraft is purchased.
